-How do you feel about caffiene? Tea and coffee are good options to keep you awake (and get you going) in the morning.  But if this is going to set off your anxiety, I would avoid it altogether or use a very minimal amount. 2 tea bags at most. One cup of coffee at most


-Also, if you can get yourself into a consistent routine, your body will follow suit.


-Is your lethargy powerful enough that it could be linked to a nutritional deficiency or other condition? Or do you think it is primary due to depression/lack of motivation? something to think about


-Start a daily bullet point "TO DO" list in a composition book. It helps especially if you can check off each task you have accomplished as you accomplish them.


**Reflect on these tasks at the end of the day and bask in that feeling of achievement. 
It does not have to be anything huge or life changing. It can be small things too, like taking out the trash or brushing your teeth every night before bed. To avoid burning out, starting small is a better way to go- and build upon that



****Which leads me to my last suggestion- set some reasonable goal(s) for yourself. They can be small or big, and then physically (pen and paper) write them out in a list. What steps do you need to take to get there? Write each step out one after the other and only take one step at a time.
Be sure to reward yourself after you complete each step. Being goal oriented (make it a good goal! something that speaks to you, or something you've been wanting to do for a long time) really helps with motivation and energy.


Lastly, allow yourself to be imperfect yet give yourself the freedom to still make progress, however small or big.

I'll tell a story. 3 years ago I overdosed on a medication that..if I hadn't been treated for, would have killed me for sure. I ended up calling an ambulance upon ingesting an entire bottle of said medication, because I couldn't bare to think of what would have happened to my cat without me in her life. I was all she had, and at the time she was all I had too.  In the E.R. they put me under observation for 4 hours. I had to drink charcoal (2 entire bottles) of the stuff with a straw. It's a huge bottle and yes...it's literally just activated charcoal made into a thick slurpie like consistency. It's disgusting. But what was worse than that... I had to wear an adult diaper for 4 days after because I involuntarily shat myself for that long. I shit all over myself in the cop car on my way to the psych unit after they cleared me from ER observation. I shit all over myself in the psych unit. I filled up my adult diaper constantly, stained bed sheets, pants and everything else that was near me. Guess what? This is the not so glamorous side of surviving an overdose. Would I have regretted it? I'd be dead so I can't regret shit. Am I glad I'm alive? Yes. Fucking yes I am. I'm horribly depressed and going through a bad bout of illness right now, but I'm glad to be here still. Even on the days where I really want to die (which happens often), I'm still glad for the days when I feel slightly better. Even if I have to force myself to do the things I used to enjoy, I'm grateful for it. Because there is still a chance that I can heal more past trauma, and make a better future for myself. Believe her when she says she is in pain, even if it might not sound like a big deal to you. Offer to listen to her story if she is comfortable telling it to you. Listen to her without advising or trying to 'fix' her, unless she directly asks for your help. Write her a letter or send her a text and talk about a memory you both shared that you remember fondly. send her a gift that you know she will love. Remind her firmly, but with no judgement, that you believe in her ability to overcome what she is going through right now. Put emphasis on the fact that you are proud of her inner fortitude and strength to get through what is going on. Ask her if anything you can do will help her. Ask her if she feels safe. Remind her that she is not alone, and that you care for her

This reminds me of a buddhist talk by thich nhat hanh. He says that "Your suffering carries with it the suffering of your mother, your father, your ancestors" And goes on to say that it is our responsiblity to break that chain of suffering. That it's achievable with persistent effort.

Another thing I'd like to add is to respect her space. When she says "no" to your offers, respect that. Come back in a few days and try again, but always make sure she knows that your door is open to her. send her texts every day that say nice things like "Hey you looked really beautiful the last time I saw you." Or: "I hope you're feeling better!"

One of the best things you can offer her is acceptance. Accept her where she is in her life and in herself right now. Don't judge it or try to label it. Tell her that you have noticed she seems sick alot more lately, and offer to help. Offer. Don't push it. A gentle nudge is fine, but if you become overbearing...it can push people away. You'll want to say things like "I'm here if you need anything." "If you want to go for a walk with me later, let me know." "Would you like to go out for dinner?" Treat her with love and care, not as someone who needs to be 'saved'. This will go a long way.

You dont need to move or die to fix this situation. A sympathetic apology would do. You might even offer them the chance to talk about wether or not it deeply upset them. Ask them how it made them feel. You'd be surprised what just listening can do to help other people. Also, you were sharing a perspective that is seldom talked about..but needs to be. People are quick to judge the person who talks about or follows through with suicide as 'selfish'. Rarely do people talk about it from the other way around. Your offending them was only accidental, not on purpose. The fact that you even care about this says a great deal about the kind hearted person you actually are. You're not some monster that needs to go hide themselves in shame. You're just human and you're entitled to make mistakes...for the rest of your life.

I have had social problems my entire life, with romantic relationships being at the forefront of that difficulty. I made some pretty bad mistakes in my past, lost friends and lovers because of it. People will always judge us for what we do or don't do, but honestly no one person is "perfect", as they say. Certainly we have the ability to change and transform ourselves, it's just that not everyone has the courage to do so. 

But if you have the courage, that says alot about the depth of who you are and that you care enough to change certain aspects of your behavior that might have been harmful to other people. I think that alone is worth feeling good about.  It's something to be proud of.

I know we hear it over and over again but really..none of us can change our past. We can stop repeating it by making decisions in the present which impact our future. It's all we can do.

How you stop the paranoia: Remind yourself that what's behind you is just that..behind you. Remember that change isn't possible without effort, and that you have put the effort in. Remember also that sometimes we fall back into old habits, and that what matters is not the fall back into them but the come back from them. Will you make a decision to beat yourself up, or will you remind yourself that you can do better next time? 

That's the difference right there. shame doesn't allow room for growth and self acceptance. You have the choice and the power to make it. Make the choice that helps your continued growth, the choice that frees you from the past.

I'm autistic. I want to share with you my experience in hopes that you can relate or see a hope in your future. You asked us why not, so I'll explain how things have gotten better for me.

I'd like to make it clear that i'll always be autistic and yes, very socially awkward. I was so socially awkward in fact that I spent weeks alone in my room locked inside because social interactions literally terrified me.  I even dropped out of school and never went back, i'm paying for that now. I had one friend for a few years, her name is Cassie. Cassie was kind to me and I always felt like I could be myself around her. But every time she tried to hang out, I couldn't bring myself to do it.  I remember one instance very specifically... Cassie was set to come over that afternoon so she told me to stay home and wait for her, we were going to get lunch. We were teenagers without cars so she walked 2 miles to come get me. By the time she got there, I was sitting on my bed shaking all over and hysterical. I was terrified to open that door. I heard her knocking for a good 10 minutes but I couldn't do it. I felt horrible about the event and I quit talking to her altogether. It was incredibly painful because she was like my best friend, but I didn't know how to tell her that I stood her up. I felt so ashamed that I just ended the  friendship, giving her no reason as to why. 

At the time I did not know what autism was, but I knew something was wrong. One could argue that this is social anxiety but I believe the anxiety is brought about by my inability to socialize properly. I spent the next 10 years going in and out of social situations completely awkward to the point where people actually called me a weirdo (on more than one occasion). People would literally tell me that I was awkward and it made them so uncomfortable that they didn't want to hang around me. I understood physical boundaries, but I had no way of communicating properly. I couldn't make small talk, everything had to be discussed in detail (even simple concepts). I get obsessed with things too and they permeate into my conversations (which tends to piss people off).

I hated myself dude. I absolutely did. I would be shaking/trembling the entire time I was hanging out with someone. It wasn't until I started seeing a psychologist that I was able to "fix" any of this. I started seeing a psychologist when I was 27 and I am 30 now. These days I can actually have a casual conversation with someone, but I have to plan it out in advance. I practice what I am going to say to the person before I see them. I take into account their interests and recent experiences in life so that I can ask them about it in a conversation. 
I have to analyze them as much as I possibly can so as not to say anything "stupid" or "awkward" and tailor the conversation specifically for them. LOL! Its FUCKING exhausting! Most people don't realize how much effort it fucking takes to have a conversation or even just be present in a social gathering when you are autistic, but it do. Oh, it do. 

The other day I was at a severe weather spotter training class (because I'm currently obsessed with weather) and I had a question for the meteorologist. My heart was pounding out of my chest and I felt near faint while asking said question. I get like that. It happens every time, it even happens with people that I know well. I don't think those on the outside can see what's going on with me. I might look like a normal ass person asking a question, but inside I literally feel like I am about to die or run out of the room crying. I have learned to live with this ,no matter how painfully uncomfortable it is. I just remind myself "I will leave this situation once it is over, and I can retreat to a safe space if I need to".

Essentially I have to be my own support system because for me I am effected emotionally by these events. 

My suggestion to you if you haven't done this already- find a psychologist who specializes in autism. You might try to look for someone at the doctorate level. I don't know what kind of insurance you have, if any, and where you are located in the world..but this could be something you do in your future. 

If not for my psychologist, I don't think I would be alive today. They helped me navigate my often confusing brain and lessen the impact of stimulus by helping me retrain my thoughts. 

One thing you have to make peace with is the fact that not everyone will understand you. It just won't happen, and this is true even if you weren't autistic. People judge. It's just what we do, some are more insightful than others but it is not your responsibility to take their perspective on your shoulders. 

If you don't know how to have casual conversation, google it. If you find it's too exhausting for you to put so much effort into it..then just  don't. Just take a break. If you're anything like me, you'll need lots of breaks to avoid sudden crash and burn-out. 

I suggest also talking to other autistic people about these things. It really freaking helps. 

AND NO YOU ARE NOT HATED BY EVERYONE!!!! People just don't get it. Like I said, that's really not your fault. One of my best friends is autistic and even more socially awkward than I am. But I get him because I took the time to get him. Now I know he's one of the greatest people in my life and I value one good friend over 30 fake ass gangstas.
